transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

I guess… I’m here because I can’t stop thinking about how I look. Mostly my hairline, and my face under the lights at work. I work in a restaurant, and it just makes me feel like I look old or… strange. People there say they don’t see it, but I do.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, grooming, or trying to fix how you look in any way?

Yeah… I do. Before my shift I’ll check the bathroom mirror a lot. I take pictures on my phone from different angles, mess with my hair, comb it forward… just trying to see if it looks okay.

Sometimes I get stuck thinking about how the guests are going to see me, and then I’m late or too worked up to go out front.
Do you think others notice or judge your appearance in the same way you do, or do you feel like it’s something only you can see?

I mean… my coworkers say they don’t see it. They say my hairline looks fine, my face looks normal.

But under the restaurant lights, I just… I can’t stop seeing it. I feel like it makes me look old, or strange. So I guess it feels like other people must notice, even if they say they don’t.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of preoccupation with perceived defects in appearance, repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, grooming), and concerns that others are judging their appearance align specifically with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). Other candidates (F40.00, F44.8) are ruled out due to the absence of primary symptoms related to phobic anxiety or dissociative/conversion disorders.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent preoccupation with perceived defects in physical appearance—primarily focused on the hairline and facial appearance—accompanied by repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, taking photos, grooming) aimed at reducing distress or conceal the perceived flaws. These symptoms cause clinically significant distress and impairment in occupational functioning, as evidenced by anxiety before shifts and difficulty engaging with guests. The concerns are not better explained by another mental disorder such as major depressive disorder or social anxiety disorder, and there is no evidence of delusional beliefs to suggest a psychotic disorder.
